rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes `input.size(3)` to `input.size(2)` on line 84, which retrieves input_width. For the fixed input shape [16, 32, 128, 128]: input.size(2) = 128 (height) and input.size(3) = 128 (width). Both dimensions are identical, so the mutated code computes exactly the same input_width value (128) as the original.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes which tensor dimension is used to determine input_width: the original uses dimension 3 (width), while the mutant uses dimension 2 (height). However, the fixed input shape is [16, 32, 128, 128], meaning height and width are both 128. Since input.size(2) == input.size(3) == 128, the computed input_width is identical in both versions. This value propagates to output_width calculation and is passed to the kernel, but since the value is the same, all downstream computations produce identical results. No value-level input manipulation can cause a difference because the shape determines the dimension sizes, not the tensor values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only be observable with non-square inputs where height ≠ width, but changing the input shape violates the testing contract. With the fixed 128x128 spatial dimensions, input.size(2) and input.size(3) always return the same value.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should consider shape-dependent equivalence when evaluating mutants. For dimension-index mutations, square tensor shapes create equivalent mutants that would only be distinguishable with different shapes. Test suites should include non-square inputs when possible to catch such bugs in development.
